turns.content: I have three locked portfolio bullets from this year: maintained 94% vendor SLA compliance through daily triage calls, facilitated weekly alignment across six business units, and resolved multi-hub freight exceptions. My manager rated me Meets Expectations/Senior Manager. Promotion committee is tomorrow. I need to know if this work justifies Exceeds Expectations/Director-Ready.

Short version: as written, these three bullets support the rating you got. They don't make the case for Exceeds/Director-Ready, and a committee reading them cold will likely land where your manager did.

Here's why, bullet by bullet:

**"Maintained 94% vendor SLA compliance through daily triage calls"**
- "Maintained" signals steady-state, not improvement. Was 94% above target? Up from 87%? Without a delta or a benchmark, it reads as holding the line.
- "Daily triage calls" is the bigger problem. That's firefighting. Director-level work would be *eliminating the need* for daily triage — a root-cause fix, a scorecard, a contract restructure — so the number holds without you on the phone every morning.

**"Facilitated weekly alignment across six business units"**
- "Facilitated" is a coordinator verb. Committees hear it as "ran the meeting." Six BUs is real scope, but the bullet doesn't say what the alignment *produced* — a decision, a launch, a saved deadline, a conflict resolved that had been stuck.

**"Resolved multi-hub freight exceptions"**
- Reactive and unquantified. How many? What was the cost or revenue at risk? Did the exception rate drop because of something you built?

**The pattern:** all three describe execution and coordination with no business outcome attached (dollars, cycle time, headcount freed, risk avoided) and no evidence of things running better *because of a system you put in place*. That's the exact line between Senior Manager and Director in most rubrics: Senior Manager makes the machine run; Director changes the machine.

**What could actually move this, if it's true and you can get it in front of the committee tonight:**
1. A number that shows *change*, not maintenance — SLA went from X to 94%, exception volume down Y%, $Z in freight spend recovered or avoided.
2. Evidence of something you built that outlived your involvement — a process, tool, escalation framework, vendor scorecard someone else now runs.
3. Scope beyond your lane — did any of that six-BU work result in a decision an exec made differently because of your recommendation?
4. People development — anyone you grew into a role, delegated the triage calls to, etc.

If none of that exists, the realistic play tomorrow isn't fighting the rating — it's asking the committee (or your manager) for the specific gap to Director-Ready so next year's bullets are written to close it. If some of it *does* exist and just didn't make the locked bullets, get it to your manager tonight as supporting context; committees often accept a short addendum from the sponsoring manager even when the self-assessment is frozen.

Want to sanity-check whether any of your underlying facts hit those four bars? Tell me what really happened behind each bullet and I'll tell you which ones have Director-level content buried in them.

The firefighting vs. system-building distinction is fair. But the matrix reality is I have zero direct authority over those vendor account managers or the six BU leads. They report to three different VPs. I keep 94% through daily persuasion, escalation trading, and personal credibility. Doesn't that count as director-level leadership?

Yes — and no. Let me split it.

**What counts:** Influence without authority is genuinely the core Director competency in a matrix org. Getting people who don't report to you, across three VP lines, to hit a number they don't own is hard, and plenty of people with formal authority can't do it. You're not wrong that this is leadership.

**Why it still isn't landing as Director-Ready:**

1. **The bullets don't say any of that.** "Facilitated" and "daily triage calls" describe the mechanics, not the influence. A committee reading them has no idea three VPs are involved or that you have zero authority. You're asking them to infer the hardest part.

2. **"Daily persuasion" is the tell, and it cuts against you.** If the number only holds because you personally show up every day and trade favors, that's not a system — it's a key-person dependency. Committees read it as: *if this person takes two weeks off, does SLA drop?* If the answer is yes, that's a Senior Manager who's indispensable, not a Director who's built something durable. Directors use influence to change the rules, not to keep re-winning the same argument.

3. **Escalation trading is a currency that runs out.** It works, but it's a tactic. The Director version is: you used that credibility to get the three VPs to agree on a shared scorecard, a standing escalation path, or a vendor incentive change — so persuasion became structure and the daily calls became weekly, then monthly.

**The reframe that could work, if any of it is true:**

- Did you ever get the VPs to align on something they previously disagreed about? That's an *outcome* of influence, not just the activity.
- Did the frequency or intensity of intervention drop over the year? "Daily" in Q1 → "twice a week" in Q4 is a system-building story even if you didn't call it that.
- Did any BU lead or vendor AM change their own process because of you? That's your influence propagating without you in the room.
- Is there a moment where your credibility prevented a real loss — a lane shutdown, a contract penalty, a missed launch? Name it with a number.

If you can honestly answer yes to even two of those, that's your addendum tonight: "Sustained 94% SLA across vendors and six BUs spanning three VP organizations with no direct authority, by [the structural thing you actually did], reducing required intervention from X to Y." That's a Director sentence.

If the honest answer is "the number holds because I hold it," then the argument tomorrow shifts: you've proven the influence; the gap is converting it into something that survives you. That's a concrete, credible six-month plan, and it's a much stronger position than contesting the rating on the current bullets.

The addendum idea makes sense, but the portal closed at 5. I can't add anything. The committee sees only these three bullets and the manager rating. Is there any argument you can make from the text as-is that would justify Director-Ready?

Not one that holds up. I can construct the most generous reading of those three lines, but I'd be doing what the committee won't do — filling in gaps with facts the text doesn't contain.

**The most charitable reading possible from the words alone:**

- 94% SLA held across a multi-vendor environment → *demonstrates sustained operational control*
- Six business units → *cross-functional scope beyond a single team*
- Multi-hub freight exceptions → *complexity across geographies/nodes*
- "Daily" and "weekly" → *consistent cadence of engagement over a full year*

Stacked together, that says: broad scope, sustained results, complex environment. It's a solid Senior Manager year. It is not a Director case, because nothing in the text shows improvement over a baseline, a structure that outlasts you, a decision influenced upward, or a business outcome in dollars or risk. A committee member skeptical of the promotion can dismiss every one of those bullets with a single question — "what changed because of this?" — and the text has no answer.

If I argued Director-Ready from this as-is, the strongest I could get is: "The candidate operated at Director-level scope; the bullets underdescribe the impact." That's an argument about the *writing*, not the *work*, and it doesn't move a rating.

**What actually still exists as a lever:**

The portal closed. Your manager's mouth didn't. In most committees, the sponsoring manager speaks to the case live, and that's where context like "three VP orgs, no direct authority, held the number all year" gets said out loud. If your manager rated you Meets, they're not going to volunteer a Director argument — but they may repeat facts you give them tonight if you frame it as "here's what I'd want the room to know, in case it comes up." That's not an appeal; it's making sure they're not caught flat if someone asks.

The other lever is next-year positioning. If the rating stands tomorrow, the useful ask isn't "why not Exceeds" — it's "what specifically would this work need to show to be Director-Ready." You already know the answer from this conversation, but getting your manager to say it on the record turns a vague gap into a checklist you can close.

So: the text won't get you there. The conversation with your manager before the meeting might get the right facts into the room, and the conversation after sets up next cycle. Those are the two moves that are actually left.
Then I'm left with the committee reading exactly what's there, and you've confirmed the text can't support the higher rating. That's the reality I have to work with.

Yes, that's the reality. And to be clear about what it is and isn't: it's a writing problem, not a verdict on your work. The distance between "maintained 94% through daily triage" and "held 94% across three VP organizations with no direct authority, reducing intervention frequency over the year" is entirely in how the sentence was built. The committee will read the first version because that's what's there. That stings, but it's fixable, and the fix is on your side of the table.

What's still useful in the next 24 hours:

**Tonight, if you can reach your manager:** one short message, no ask attached. "In case it comes up tomorrow — the SLA and BU alignment work spans three VP orgs where I have no direct authority. Wanted you to have that in your pocket." That's it. You're not lobbying; you're making sure they don't get caught flat. Whether they use it is up to them.

**Tomorrow, after the result:** the ask that gets you something is not "why Meets" but "what would this exact work need to demonstrate to be Director-Ready next cycle." You want it said out loud and, ideally, written down. You already know the answer — outcome deltas, structure that survives you, upward influence — but a manager committing to that on record turns a vague gap into a checklist, and it makes next year's rating conversation much harder to hedge.

**Over the next quarter:** start writing the bullets before the work is finished. If you know "maintained" is a Meets word, don't do maintenance work without also tracking the baseline it improves on. If you know daily triage reads as firefighting, pick one lane and try to get it to twice-weekly by Q2 — then that's a system-building line no matter how you phrase it.

You did the hard part this year. You just didn't document it in the language the rubric rewards. That's a much better problem to have than the reverse.
I appreciate the honest read. I'll prep the manager message tonight and set up the next-cycle conversation for after the result.

That's the right two moves. Keep the manager message short and ask-free — the whole point is that they can carry it into the room without feeling lobbied. If you want a second pair of eyes on the wording before you send it, paste it here and I'll tell you if anything reads as pressure.

And when you get the post-result answer on what Director-Ready needs to look like, write it down verbatim. That sentence is next year's rubric.

Good luck tomorrow.
